sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Fúxī** (*fuxi*) — The First Teacher — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Culture, Writing, Divination". The name means "Hidden one"[^1].

Fúxī is where Chinese civilization says it learned to think: the sage-king who looked up at the heavens, down at the earth, and at the markings on birds and beasts — and abstracted the eight trigrams, the first writing of pattern itself.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Fúxī** and serves its temple at [fúxī.com](https://xn--fx-rka1r.com). The restoration preserves the accent on ú and the macron on ī — distinctive features the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *fuxi* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: I Ching (Yijing / Book of Changes), Chinese Text Project, 1000 BCE.
Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), Sima Qian; Chinese Text Project, 91 BCE.
Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Chinese characters as **伏羲**. Etymologically it means "Hidden one"[^1].

The ASCII form *fuxi* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Fúxī** recovers both the stress accent and the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves the accent on ú and the macron on ī — distinctive features the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **f** → **F** — Same, capitalized
- **u** → **ú** — Stress on u
- **x** → **x** — Same
- **i** → **ī** — Long vowel

The project holds the domain **fúxī.com** (xn--fx-rka1r.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), Sima Qian; Chinese Text Project, 91 BCE.
Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/fu˧˥ ɕi˥/** — Mandarin (Hanyu Pinyin with tones).[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: foo-shee, rising tone on fu, high level on xi.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — 伏羲
- **Variant writing** — 庖犧 (Páoxī)
- **Owned form** — Fúxī

Fúxī 伏羲 carries the rising tone on both syllables in Mandarin; older romanizations write Fu-hsi. The first graph 伏 suggests "to subdue, to prostrate," the second 羲 a sacrificial term — a name older than its etymologies, borne by the first of the Three August Ones. The older romanization Fu-hsi records the same syllables; pinyin's x is the alveolo-palatal fricative of modern Mandarin.

sources.citation: I Ching (Yijing / Book of Changes), Chinese Text Project, 1000 BCE.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is written in Chinese characters as **伏羲**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *fuxi* and the PuniCodex restoration **Fúxī** are measured: the restoration preserves both its pitch accent and its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

Written 伏羲: fú (subdue; the man-radical with the hound) plus xī (the ancient graph for sacrificial breath). The compound is attested from Warring States texts onward — the name predates any agreed reading of it, which is itself a mark of antiquity.

sources.citation: I Ching (Yijing / Book of Changes), Chinese Text Project, 1000 BCE.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Fúxī is where Chinese civilization says it learned to think: the sage-king who looked up at the heavens, down at the earth, and at the markings on birds and beasts — and abstracted the eight trigrams, the first writing of pattern itself.[^1]

### The Eight Trigrams

Bāguà: broken and unbroken lines in threes — the binary alphabet of the Yìjīng, attributed to his observation.

### The Net

He taught the people to knot cords into nets — fishing, hunting, and the technology of the snare.

### The Serpent Bodies

Han art shows him and Nǚwā as serpents intertwined — the primal pair, measuring square and compass in hand.

### Marriage

He instituted the rites of marriage and the bride-price of deer skins — order after the flood.

sources.citation: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), Sima Qian; Chinese Text Project, 91 BCE.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Fúxī concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The trigrams** — Pattern abstracted from nature — the seed of all Chinese correlative thought
- **The carpenter's square** — His emblem in Han art: the earth-measurer's tool (Nǚwā holds the compass of heaven)
- **The dragon-horse** — The creature from the Yellow River whose markings revealed the diagram

sources.citation: I Ching (Yijing / Book of Changes), Chinese Text Project, 1000 BCE.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Fúxī's myths are all acts of notation: he does not fight or flee — he observes, abstracts, and teaches. He is the culture-bringer as draftsman.[^1]

### Reading the World (The Diagram)

The Yìjīng's Great Treatise records the founding act: Fúxī looked up and contemplated the images of heaven, looked down and contemplated the patterns of earth, contemplated the markings of birds and beasts and the order of the near at hand — and from all three made the eight trigrams, "to comprehend the powers of the spirits and to classify the natures of the ten thousand things." Writing, mathematics, and divination begin as one gesture of attention.[^2]

### The Dragon-Horse's Map (The River)

Later tradition gives the revelation a courier: a dragon-horse rose from the Yellow River bearing on its back the Hétú, the River Chart — the arrangement of numbers and marks from which Fúxī drew the trigrams. Paired with the Luò River Writing that inspired the Great Plan, the Chart made the Yellow River itself the first text of Chinese civilization.

### The Brother-Sister Marriage (The Flood)

In the flood myth recorded among the Miao and in Tang collections, Fúxī and Nǚwā alone survive the waters, taking refuge on Mount Kūnlún. Brother and sister, they divine heaven's will by rolling millstones and watching smoke columns join — and consent to marry, repopulating the drowned world. The myth explains both marriage's institution and humanity's second beginning.

### Nets, Music, and Domestication (The Arts)

The tradition credits him with the survival-arts in sequence: knotting cords into nets for fishing and hunting, keeping domestic animals (hence one reading of his name, "subduer of beasts"), making the thirty-five-stringed se zither, and fixing the marriage rites. Civilization, in his legend, is a curriculum — and he is its whole faculty.

sources.citation: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), Sima Qian; Chinese Text Project, 91 BCE.
Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
He heads most lists of the Three August Ones (Sānhuáng), paired inseparably with Nǚwā — their intertwined serpent forms in Han art echoing, scholars note, the union of measure and generation. Daoist tradition absorbed him as a revealer of the trigrams to the immortal lineages; Confucian tradition kept him as the first historian of pattern. The serpent-pair iconography has been compared by art historians with intertwined pairs from Egypt to India — diffusion debated, the resemblance celebrated.[^1]

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[guanyin|Guānyīn]], [[long|Lóng]], [[mengpo|Méngpó]], [[nuwa|Nǚwā]], and [[pangu|Pángǔ]].

sources.citation: I Ching (Yijing / Book of Changes), Chinese Text Project, 1000 BCE.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Every reading of the Yìjīng — the book that shaped Confucian statecraft, Daoist alchemy, and Leibniz's binary arithmetic — begins with his act of looking. The eight trigrams appear on the flag of South Korea; the River Chart structures a millennium of cosmological diagrams; and "Fúxī" remains the standard icon for the inventor-ancestor in Chinese cultural memory, the answer to the question of where pattern-thinking began.[^1]

sources.citation: I Ching (Yijing / Book of Changes), Chinese Text Project, 1000 BCE.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
The Wu Liang shrine reliefs (2nd century CE, Shandong) show Fúxī and Nǚwā with serpent bodies entwined, square and compass raised — the canonical image, replicated across Han tomb art from Sichuan to Xinjiang (the famous Astana cemetery banner). The myth's textual archaeology runs from the Zhuangzi and Xunzi mentions to the Tang's flood-cycle records: a steady accretion from sage-king to cosmic progenitor, all preserved in the transmitted classics.[^1]

His cult anchored in the northwest: the **Fúxī temple at Tianshui** (Gansu), founded under the Ming, claims his birthplace and keeps his statue with the trigrams; the city still holds his festival. The **Huáiyáng** tomb-temple in Henan — the Tàihào Líng, 'tomb of the Great Bright One' — has drawn one of China's largest temple fairs for centuries, a month of pilgrimage in the second lunar month. Both sites make the same claim the classics do: that the pattern-reader of the Yellow River was buried and is honoured on its banks.

sources.citation: I Ching (Yijing / Book of Changes), Chinese Text Project, 1000 BCE.
The Tianshui and Huaiyang temple records; Birrell, Chinese Mythology.

sections.label: Classical Texts
sections.body:
The first teacher's titles span three thousand years of state ritual.

- **Tàihào (太皞)** — 'the Great Bright One'; his oldest title, paired with the eastern direction.
- **Páoxī (庖犧)** — the variant writing of his name, 'he of the kitchen/sacrifice'; the domestication of animals in a graph.
- **Sānhuáng zhī shǒu** — 'first of the Three August Ones'; his place in the canonical succession.
- **Lóngshī (龍師)** — 'Dragon Master'; the title from the tradition that he named his officers for dragons.
- **Bāguà zhī shǐzǔ** — 'Ancestor of the Eight Trigrams'; the diviners' title for the pattern's first reader.

sources.citation: Yijing, Xici zhuan; Shiji (Sānhuáng traditions); Birrell, Chinese Mythology.

sections.label: Daoist Sources
sections.body: Daoism kept him as the patron of revelation: the Daozang's cosmological treatises credit Fúxī with the trigrams that the alchemical classics (the *Zhouyi Cantongqi* above all) elaborate into the machinery of inner alchemy — qian and kun, the cauldron's firing times, the whole symbolic calculus. In the Daoist sacred histories he figures among the pre-Laozi sages who received heaven's patterns before writing existed, and the trigrams are read as the Daozang's oldest scripture: the eight signs that precede all books.

sources.citation: Zhouyi Cantongqi; Daozang cosmological treatises.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Buddhist Sources
sections.body: Buddhist literature engages Fúxī mainly at the boundary of the two teachings: apologetic treatises of the Six Dynasties and Tang (the *Mouzi Lihuolun* tradition and its successors) discuss the Chinese sage-kings when measuring the dharma against native wisdom, and the Chan genealogies cite the trigram-sages as proof that China had its own way before Bodhidharma. He is thus a fixed reference in the oldest East Asian interreligious conversation: the Buddhist case that awakening and the sages' pattern-reading are one.

sources.citation: Mouzi Lihuolun tradition; the Chan genealogical records.

sections.label: Calligraphy & Script
sections.body: 伏羲: the first graph (伏) is the man-radical with the hound — "to subdue, to lie down"; the second (羲) is the ancient sacrificial graph with 羊 above 兮, a character used almost nowhere else in the language. In seal script the pair is a masterclass in archaic structure; the alternative old writing 庖犧 ("kitchen-sacrifice," punning on his domestication of animals) survives in the classics. Stele rubbings of the Three-August-One inscriptions and the Huaiyang temple's great calligraphy keep the name as a writing subject in its own right.

sources.citation: Shuowen Jiezi (羲); the Huaiyang temple inscriptions.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Fúxī is the patron of the second look — the one that sees not the thing but the pattern. His trigrams are only broken and unbroken lines, yet a civilization read everything in them for three thousand years. He asks the observer's question: what in the world are you willing to look at long enough that it begins, at last, to read back?

Leibniz saw the trigrams and recognized binary arithmetic; the information age looked again and found the whole grammar of bits — the broken and unbroken line as zero and one. Whether or not the old sage intended the code, his lesson stands: the world's patterns are legible to whoever looks long enough, and three lines, honestly observed, can hold a civilization's worth of distinctions. The first technology was attention.

The tradition says he looked at the horse's markings and the turtle's shell and saw not omen but order — the world already written, waiting for a reader. Every analysis since, from the Yìjīng's commentaries to the database schema, is his gesture repeated: reduce the world to its honest marks, and the marks will begin to answer.[^1]

sources.citation: I Ching (Yijing / Book of Changes), Chinese Text Project, 1000 BCE.
